Should the blob fee market be fixed?

Your voice matters! Should we revive symmetric fee adjustments in the next hard fork? Like, RT, and like/comment in the forum thread above to show the devs we care about Ethereum's long-term health and fixing the blob fee market!

The good news? This isn't theoretical—there's an EIP drafted and proposed solution! It's a relatively simple change that could be included in a future hard fork with minimal disruption. Check the discussion: https://t.co/w8ZvZGtv09 #FixTheBlobMarket

L2s initially pushed against this—lower fees suit them well. But Ethereum isn't just about L2s. Validators, users, and long-term network health matter too. Sometimes the most important improvements aren't the loudest requested.

The solution is clear: symmetric fee adjustments. Fees rise and fall at the same rate. This creates:

·  Predictable costs
·  More balanced blob usage
·  Less volatility in blob fees
·  Stronger validator economics

It'd be a massive win!

Blobs power Layer 2s, Ethereum's scalability backbone, but the current asymmetric fee system is lopsided—fees drop fast, yet rise slowly. Result? Unpredictable spikes, inefficient resource allocation, volatility in blob usage, and too low blob fees. 📉

4/ Tokens uniquely solve this problem through ILMs, which we define as contributor-owned marketplaces where the unit of work is a verifiable task, settled instantly over crypto rails.

3/ These new organizations still depend on non-software inputs: data, labeling, evaluation, physical deployment, domain expertise, edge-case handling. Many of these inputs are intermittent, global, and hard to hire for in a traditional way.

tweets.text: @jonaswillett1 @thecollectiv3e sir this is not the west village
@lex_node @banteg Unfortunately true

So no — I'm not worried about AI replacing humans.
I'm excited for what gets built next. 🚀

The question was never "will humans still matter?"
It's "what new forms will human attention take next?"
We've never gotten that answer wrong. We've only been unable to see it in advance.

AI will displace tasks. Absolutely.
But it will also hand billions of people new tools — and some of them will build things we cannot imagine yet.
That's the pattern. That's always been the pattern.

Geoffrey Miller argued in Spent that most of what we consume is really a signal.
We're buying access to the minds, taste, and status of other people.
Tech changes the medium. It doesn't change that drive.

Here's the deeper principle:
Human attention is the scarce resource that never goes away.
Tech can automate tasks. It cannot automate desire — our appetite for things made by, curated by, or connected to other humans.

Nobody in 1990 predicted the internet would create:
→ Influencers → Podcast empires → UX designers → SEO agencies → SaaS companies → Discord communities
The list is endless. And it's still growing.

What actually happened?
The freed-up humans — often enabled by the very tech that displaced them — built entirely new products and industries.
Industries that were literally unimaginable beforehand.

Will AI replace humans?
Every wave of technology replaces humans at a task. The printing press, the loom, the spreadsheet.
Each one triggered the same fear: "What will people do for work?"
